question: A 47-year-old man comes to the physician because of abdominal pain and foul-smelling, watery diarrhea for several days. He has not had nausea, vomiting, or blood in the stool. He has a history of alcohol use disorder and recently completed a 7-day course of clindamycin for pneumonia. He has not traveled out of the United States. Which of the following toxins is most likely to be involved in the pathogenesis of this patient's symptoms?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Clindamycin administration -> disruption of normal gut flora -> Clostridioides difficile overgrowth -> Clostridioides difficile cytotoxin production -> patient's symptoms -> Clostridioides difficile cytotoxin -> damage to intestinal epithelial cells -> abdominal pain and foul-smelling, watery diarrhea -> Clostridioides difficile infection -> Clostridioides difficile infection -> Clostridioides difficile cytotoxin as the likely toxin involved -> 95%
analysis: Given the patient's history of recent clindamycin use and symptoms of abdominal pain and foul-smelling diarrhea, the most likely toxin involved in this case is Clostridioides difficile cytotoxin. Clindamycin is a known risk factor for Clostridium difficile infection due to its disruption of the normal gut flora, leading to overgrowth of C. difficile and toxin production.
